name: Global Fronts
blurb: Problems no region owns: emissions, plastics, nitrogen, wildlife trade, subsidies and the high seas. They spread along trade routes, so they are won with treaties and rules; the last mission shows a treaty that worked.

issues.title: The Carbon Budget

drivers.name: Tipping points such as forest dieback and ocean-circulation change
Seasons out of step with flowers and pollinators

fact.text: The Global Carbon Budget 2025 projected 38.1 billion tonnes of fossil CO2 emissions for 2025, about 1% more than in 2024 and a record high. It put the remaining carbon budget for a 50% chance of limiting warming to 1.5°C at 170 billion tonnes of CO2, nearly exhausted: around four years at 2025 emission levels.
fact.source: Global Carbon Project, Global Carbon Budget 2025, Earth System Science Data (13 May 2026)

issues.realWorld: Cut the energy you use at home and when you travel, back policies that phase out fossil fuels, and ask where your bank and pension invest.

issues.title: The Plastics Treaty

drivers.name: No agreed global rule on production

sites: A garbage patch in an ocean gyre

fact.text: Talks in Geneva on a global plastic pollution treaty ended on 15 August 2025 with no agreed text, after the chair’s 13 August draft was rejected by many countries.
fact.source: Down To Earth, on the Geneva plastics treaty talks (INC-5.2)

issues.realWorld: Choose reusable over single-use plastic, support a legally binding global plastics treaty, and join a local cleanup.

issues.title: The Nitrogen Problem

drivers.name: Fertiliser applied beyond what crops use
Drained wetlands that no longer filter water

sites: A river basin downstream of farmland

fact.text: A 2014 study found that only 47% of the reactive nitrogen added to the world’s cropland is converted into harvested products, and that more than half is lost to the environment. Our World in Data likewise reports that less than half of the nutrients applied as fertiliser are taken up by crops globally.
fact.source: Lassaletta et al., Environmental Research Letters (2014)

issues.realWorld: Waste less food, eat a little less meat and dairy, and support farms and policies that cut fertiliser losses.

issues.title: The Routes of Wildlife Crime

drivers.name: Global demand for scales, horn, ivory and pets
Disease crossing from wildlife to people

fact.text: The UNODC World Wildlife Crime Report 2024 analysed over 140,000 records of wildlife seizures from 2015 to 2021, which document illegal trade in 162 countries and territories affecting around 4,000 plant and animal species.

issues.realWorld: Never buy products made from wild animals or plants without legal proof of origin, report suspicious online wildlife sales, and support the groups that train customs and rangers.

issues.title: Paying for the Damage

drivers.name: Subsidies for destructive fishing and farming

sites: A subsidised mine and road corridor

fact.text: The IMF’s page on fossil fuel subsidies puts explicit subsidies in 2024 at $0.73 trillion (0.6 percent of global GDP) and implicit subsidies at $6.7 trillion (5.8 percent of global GDP).
fact.source: International Monetary Fund, fossil fuel subsidies

issues.realWorld: Ask your representatives to redirect harmful subsidies, and check claims of “net zero” and “carbon neutral” against independent sources before you trust them.

issues.title: 30×30 on the High Seas

drivers.name: No rules for protected areas on the high seas

fact.text: A landmark treaty to safeguard biodiversity in the high seas came into effect on 17 January 2026, with more than 80 ratifications at that point; supporters link it to the aim of bringing 30% of the oceans under formal protection by 2030.
fact.source: United Nations Treaty Collection, BBNJ Agreement (entry into force 17 January 2026)

also.source: High Seas Alliance press release (16 January 2026)
World Resources Institute, High Seas Treaty explainer

issues.realWorld: Ask your government to ratify and fund the High Seas Treaty, and choose seafood from fisheries certified as sustainable.

issues.title: The Ozone Success Story

drivers.name: A treaty enforced and strengthened over time

fact.text: A UN-backed assessment published in October 2026 projects the near-global ozone layer back at 1980 values around 2040 and the Antarctic during the 2060s, provided countries keep complying with the Montreal Protocol, which was signed in September 1987.
fact.source: WMO/UNEP Scientific Assessment of Ozone Depletion: 2026 (October 2026)

also.source: UNEP Ozone Secretariat, Final Act of the 1987 Montreal conference

issues.realWorld: Have old fridges, freezers and air-conditioners disposed of through a recycler that recovers their refrigerant, so the gases are not vented.

issues.title: Methane from oil, gas and farms

drivers.name: Leaks from oil and gas wells
